guide.title: Unit 5: Commentary, coherence, and precise language: review guide
guide.intro: Small choices hold an argument together: commentary that explains evidence, transitions that show how ideas relate, and modifiers that make claims precise. This unit practices recognizing and making those choices.

sections.title: Commentary and the line of reasoning
body: Commentary explains how evidence supports a claim and connects it to the thesis. Without commentary, evidence is just a fact sitting on the page.
Maintaining a line of reasoning means each paragraph keeps returning to the same central idea, developing it rather than drifting to a new one.
points: After each piece of evidence, explain why it matters.
Commentary often begins: “This shows…,” “Because of this…”

sections.title: Unity, coherence, and transitions
body: Transitions signal relationships: addition (also, furthermore), contrast (however, yet), cause (therefore, as a result), example (for instance), concession (although, granted).
Choose the transition that names the actual relationship between two ideas; a wrong transition misleads readers about the reasoning.
points: Repeated key words and pronouns also create coherence.

sections.title: Modifiers, word choice, and perspective
body: Modifiers (often, rarely, most, some, probably) qualify a claim, making it more precise and more defensible. Absolute words (always, never, everyone) are easy to refute.
Word choice also conveys the writer's perspective and tone: “the policy gambled” and “the policy tested” describe the same act with different attitudes.
points: Qualifiers can strengthen an argument by making it accurate.

example.prompt: Add commentary: “Students who eat breakfast at school miss fewer days, according to the district's data.”
example.solution: Commentary: “Because attendance is the first step toward learning, a free breakfast program would do more than feed students: it would bring them into the classroom where every other effort begins.”

misconceptions: Commentary explains what evidence shows and why it matters.
The transition must match the relationship between the ideas.
Accurate qualifiers make a claim harder to refute.
Words with similar meanings can carry different connotations.

passages.title: Passage 1: Murals and the city
text: (1) When the city commissioned murals for the underpass on Grant Avenue, many residents called it a waste. The underpass had long been dim and covered with graffiti, and few people walked through it after dark.

(2) Two years later, foot traffic through the underpass has roughly doubled, according to counts by a neighborhood group. Shops on both sides report more evening customers. The murals did not make the underpass safer by themselves, but they made it a place people chose to walk, and more people walking made it feel safer still.
(3) Murals will not solve every problem a neighborhood faces. Still, for a modest cost, they can turn a passage people avoid into one they use.

passages.title: Passage 2: In defense of boredom
text: (1) We treat boredom as a problem to be solved, usually with a screen. Yet boredom may be one of the more useful feelings we have.

(2) Boredom is a signal: it tells us that what we are doing does not engage us. Researchers who study it suggest that this discomfort often pushes people to look for something new. A bored child invents a game; a bored adult sketches, tinkers, or daydreams a solution to a problem at work.
(3) When we answer every flicker of boredom by reaching for a phone, we silence the signal before it can do its work. The point is not to seek boredom, but to stop running from it quite so fast.
passages.attribution: Written for StudySprint by its editors. It describes research on boredom in general terms rather than quoting a specific study.

passages.title: Draft 1: A student paragraph about a recycling program
text: The following is a draft of a student's paragraph for the school newspaper. It may need revision.

(1) Our school started a recycling program in September. (2) ____, the cafeteria now sends far less trash to the landfill. (3) Many students still throw bottles in the regular bins. (4) The program needs clearer labels on its bins. (5) ____, the student council could post signs showing what belongs in each bin.
passages.attribution: Written for StudySprint by its editors.
passages.licenseOrRights: Original text written for StudySprint; it is not taken or adapted from any College Board exam.

passages.title: Draft 2: A student paragraph about after-school jobs
text: The following is a draft of a student's paragraph for an essay about teenagers and work. It may need revision.

(1) After-school jobs always hurt students' grades. (2) A survey at our school found that students working more than twenty hours a week reported lower grades than students who did not work. (3) Students who worked fewer hours reported grades similar to non-working students. (4) Jobs teach responsibility.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best states the passage's main claim?
choices: The underpass was dim and covered with graffiti before the city acted
Murals solve the problems a neighborhood faces, including crime and empty shops
Shops on Grant Avenue have more evening customers than before
Murals can, for a modest cost, turn an avoided passage into one people use
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 states the claim that the evidence in paragraph 2 supports.
choiceExplanations: That's background about the underpass, not the claim.
The writer explicitly says murals “will not solve every problem.”
That's evidence for the claim, not the claim itself.

choices: a contrast: despite the limitation just stated, the claim still holds
an example of the limitation that is stated in the sentence just before it
a new topic: the cost of the murals
a cause of the limitation stated in the previous sentence
questions.explanation: “Still” moves from a concession (murals won't solve everything) to the writer's position.
choiceExplanations: It doesn't introduce an example; it turns back to the claim.
The topic stays the same.
It doesn't show a cause; it signals contrast.

questions.prompt: The last sentence of paragraph 2 (“The murals did not make the underpass safer by themselves…”) mainly
choices: introduces new statistics about crime in the underpass
explains how the evidence supports the claim without overstating it
contradicts the passage's claim that the murals made a real difference
describes the murals' colors and subjects for readers
questions.explanation: It is commentary: it interprets the foot-traffic numbers and the shop reports, explaining the mechanism carefully.
choiceExplanations: No new statistics appear, and crime figures aren't given.
It supports the claim with a careful explanation.
The murals' appearance isn't described anywhere in the passage.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of the words “roughly” (paragraph 2) and “modest” (paragraph 3)?
choices: They qualify the claims, so the writer sounds careful and the claims more defensible
They shift the tone from serious to playful, so readers relax
They exaggerate the murals' success to win over doubtful residents
They express the writer's doubt that murals can work in other city neighborhoods
questions.explanation: Precise qualifiers keep the claims accurate, which builds credibility with skeptical readers.
choiceExplanations: The tone stays measured and serious.
They do the opposite of exaggerating.
The writer still clearly supports murals and doesn't discuss other places.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's main claim?
choices: Phones should be banned from homes and schools to protect boredom
Children should be made bored more often so that they will learn to invent their own games
Boredom is always pleasant once people stop fighting it
People should stop rushing to escape boredom, which can push them toward new ideas
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the point is not to seek boredom but to stop running from it, because of its usefulness.
choiceExplanations: The writer doesn't call for a ban; the advice is to stop running from boredom.
The writer says “the point is not to seek boredom.”
The writer calls boredom a discomfort.

questions.prompt: In paragraph 1, the word “may” in “boredom may be one of the more useful feelings” serves to
choices: introduce a counterargument the writer will answer
qualify the claim so it is more defensible
show that the writer is certain of the claim
change the subject from boredom to feelings
questions.explanation: “May” and “more useful” make a measured claim rather than an absolute one.
choiceExplanations: It isn't a counterargument; it limits the writer's own claim.
“May” signals possibility, not certainty.
The subject stays the same.

questions.prompt: How does paragraph 2 connect to paragraph 1?
choices: It contradicts paragraph 1 by showing that boredom is uncomfortable for people
It explains why boredom is useful, supporting the claim in paragraph 1
It begins a new argument about creativity at work
It repeats paragraph 1 in different words, adding nothing new
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 develops the claim by describing boredom as a signal that prompts new activity.
choiceExplanations: It supports paragraph 1; the discomfort is part of how boredom helps.
Work is one example among several, not a new argument.
It adds an explanation and examples.

questions.prompt: In paragraph 3, the writer says we “silence the signal before it can do its work.” What is the effect of this wording?
choices: It extends the image of boredom as a signal, suggesting phones cut off something useful
It introduces a technical term from the research on boredom that the writer mentioned earlier
It shifts the passage's tone to anger at phone companies
It suggests that boredom is a dangerous signal that people should silence
questions.explanation: Continuing the “signal” metaphor ties the conclusion to paragraph 2's reasoning.
choiceExplanations: “Silence the signal” extends the writer's own image; it isn't a technical term.
The tone remains reflective, and phone companies aren't mentioned.
The passage presents boredom as useful and argues against silencing it.

In contrast
However

questions.prompt: The writer wants to add commentary after sentence (2) that connects the evidence to the paragraph's point. Which choice is best?
choices: Recycling was invented many years ago, and many towns across the whole country have run programs like ours for decades.
That drop shows the program works when students use it, which is why getting the rest of the bottles sorted matters.
Trash from the cafeteria is collected on Tuesdays and Fridays by a private hauling company.
The landfill is outside of town, about ten miles from the school, near the old quarry.
questions.explanation: This explains what the evidence shows and links it to the problem the paragraph goes on to address.
choiceExplanations: This is unrelated background that doesn't explain the evidence.
This is an unrelated detail.
This is an unrelated detail.

questions.prompt: Sentence (1) overstates the claim. Which revision best fits the evidence in sentences (2) and (3)?
choices: After-school jobs never hurt students' grades, however long the hours.
All after-school jobs are bad for students' grades.
Working long hours after school can hurt students' grades.
Jobs are a part of life for many teenagers.
questions.explanation: The survey shows lower grades only for students working many hours; the qualifiers “long hours” and “can” match that evidence.
choiceExplanations: This contradicts the survey.
This is even broader than the original.
This makes no claim about grades.

questions.prompt: Which sentence would best follow sentence (3) as commentary?
choices: The survey was given in October to students in each grade at our school.

Many of the students who work after school have jobs at local restaurants.
questions.explanation: It interprets the contrast between (2) and (3) and connects it to the paragraph's point.
choiceExplanations: This is a minor fact without interpretation.
Siblings' jobs are irrelevant to the point about hours.
This is an unrelated detail.

questions.prompt: The writer wants to describe the survey results precisely. Which wording is most accurate?
choices: students' grades collapsed once they began working after school
every student who worked more than twenty hours failed
students working over twenty hours a week tended to report lower grades
working students proved that after-school jobs ruin students' school performance
questions.explanation: “Tended to report” matches what a survey of self-reported grades can show.
choiceExplanations: “Collapsed” exaggerates the evidence, which shows only a tendency.
The survey shows lower grades, not that every such student failed.
A survey doesn't “prove” this, and it overgeneralizes.
